newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew seen standing down after saving ship.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew seen standing down after saving ship.

text.p: The accident-prone crew of Russia's Mir space station finally arrested their crazy tumble through space on Friday, locking the crippled ship's solar panels onto the Sun and switching the lights back on.

But the latest calamity, caused by a weary crewman crashing the on-board computer on Thursday, seems to have convinced controllers effectively to stand down the three cosmonauts, one of whom now has heart trouble, and wait for a relief crew to repair damage caused in a near-fatal collision last month.

Deputy mission director Sergei Krikalyov told reporters it was "very likely" the risky and complex rewiring job, already put off until next week because of commander Vasily Tsibliyev's stress-induced palpitations, would now have to wait until after the relief crew reached Mir on August 7.
Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin are due to return to Earth on August 26. British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale is to go home aboard a U.S. Shuttle in September.

A meeting of officials at Mission Control outside Moscow on Monday may decide, however, that their missions are already all but over, leaving them serving out the rest of their time on the stricken station as little more than caretakers.

Russian officials, whose agency depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep the post-Soviet space industry aloft, have resisted suggestions the three abandon ship immediately. An empty Mir would soon expire and crash back to Earth.

Two fresh Russian cosmonauts, Pavel Vinogradov and Anatoly Solovyov, are already in training at Star City near Moscow for the dangerous job of entering the airless Spektr module involved in last month's collision. They will have to mend cables cut after the accident and make a spacewalk to patch the puncture.
Mir has been limping around on half power for the past three weeks, forcing the present crew to abandon their experiments and live a highly restricted, twilight existence.

If Lazutkin and Foale are told to abandon plans to make the cable repairs themselves, then officials said French scientist Leopold Eyharts would probably no longer fly with Solovyov and Vinogradov when they blast off on August 5.
On Friday, Mission Control gave the Mir crew the day off after their hair-raising 24 hours with only minimal power.

"We have decided to allow them to rest," mission director Solovyov said, giving the three men the chance to watch videos, read or listen to music after the stress of the previous day. They might even be able to talk to their wives.

NASA astronaut Leroy Chiao told Reuters at Mission Control that they were most likely to spend some time just looking at their home planet. "The most relaxing thing to do is to look out the window," he said. "It is a unique experience."
Lazutkin, 39, toiled through the night to reconnect most of Mir's life-support systems after one cosmonaut -- officials will not say who -- pulled out a cable and crashed the computer.
"All microclimate systems are working completely normally. The conditions are completely comfortable," Solovyov said.
The computer crash disabled a gyro system that keeps Mir's solar panels lined up on the Sun, sending the power supply to a minimum and forcing the crew to shut down all but vital systems.

The panels were being held in alignment by electronically controlled motors as Mir's batteries recharged. The gyroscope system, which uses no fuel at all, was to be reconnected late on Friday. The remaining systems can then be hooked up again.
By the end of the day Mir should be back to the condition it was in on Wednesday, when the experienced Tsibliyev, 43, was taken off the repairs and Foale, 40, asked to back up Lazutkin.
Solovyov, who has had some harsh words for the crew during radio link-ups, said the problems had not been in vain and did not mean a loss of prestige for Russia's space programme.
"This has been a very complicated mission with many stressful situations," he told reporters. "This crew had an irregular situation practically from the day they got on board."
Lazutkin, who is on his first space flight, and Tsibliyev had to cope with a serious fire in February.
"Unpleasantness awaits anyone who opens up new frontiers," Solovyov said. "Yes, we had these difficulties but the ability to overcome such difficulties raises our prestige."
